patch.value: Reconciliation proves an artifact is attested but never that it came from the commit about to be tagged

The release step treats a publish as already done when the version exists on the registry and its dist.attestations field is non-empty. Neither read says which source commit produced that artifact. The consequence is not hypothetical: this fleet has repeatedly published a version and then failed to push its tag, because the tag push raced branch protection. A later run computing the same date-derived version finds the coordinate occupied and attested, reconciles, and tags its own HEAD. The git tag and the GitHub release then describe source that the immutable tarball on the registry does not contain, and the release notes describe changes that are not in the published artifact. The attestation makes this worse rather than better, because a bundle produced by the earlier commit satisfies a check that only asks whether one exists. Reconciliation must compare identity, not presence: resolve the attestation bundle for the exact version and require its recorded source commit to equal the commit being tagged, refusing when they differ instead of tagging around the mismatch. Raised independently by Greptile as two P1 security findings on the attestation wave, on pm-csv PR 87.

value.author: claude
value.text: CodeRabbit reached the same conclusion independently on pm-brief and researched the mechanism, which saves the design step. There is no single npm command that verifies the binding. The registry exposes the signed bundle at GET https://registry.npmjs.org/-/npm/v1/attestations/NAME@VERSION, which returns a Sigstore bundle carrying an in-toto statement. Three fields in it answer the question this gate needs: the subject digest, which must match the tarball the registry is serving; the build definition's repository, which must be this repository; and the recorded source commit, which must equal the commit about to be tagged. npm audit signatures is not a substitute, because it checks registry signatures rather than the provenance predicate. The refusal must therefore name which of the three mismatched, so an operator can tell an unrelated artifact from a stale one.
